chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Nadr, from 'Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Basir al-Makfuf, who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting person: when does food become forbidden for him? He said, 'When the dawn appears like the white sheet (al-qubtiyyah al-bayda').

I said: And when does the prayer become permissible? He said, 'When it is like that (i.e., at the same time).' I said: Am I not in the time from that hour until the sun rises? He said, 'No, we only count it as the prayer of the children (early/naive prayer).'
Then he said, 'It was not commendable for a man to pray in the mosque and then return to awaken his family and children (for Fajr).'

key_terms.الْقُبْطِيَّةِ الْبَيْضَاءِ: The white sheet (a specific visual description of early dawn light)
key_terms.صَلَاةَ الصِّبْيَانِ: The prayer of the children (referring to early/naive prayer time)

ai.seo_question: When does the fasting time begin according to the appearance of dawn?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the precise moment of *Fajr al-Sadiq* (true dawn), marked by the 'white sheet' (*al-qubtiyyah al-bayda*), which triggers both the prohibition of food and the onset of obligatory Fajr prayer. The Imam distinguishes this from *Fajr al-Kadhib* (false dawn), noting that praying during the earlier interval is considered the 'prayer of children' (*salat al-sibyan*), a term often used in Shia jurisprudence to denote a time of lesser obligation or preparatory status. Furthermore, it highlights the social etiquette of the time, where praying in the mosque before waking the family was not deemed fully commendable, reflecting the communal nature of early morning worship.
